vignette:
Trang Nguyen was 71 when she finally came to describe, in a measured but strained way, what had been happening to her for years. A divorced financial analyst living alone in a small condo near her office in California, she had built a life around precision, routines, and long hours at her desk, yet even now her world felt narrowed to only a few places that she experienced as truly safe: her apartment, her office during daylight, and her car if the doors were locked. Anything beyond that felt exposed. Night was especially difficult. After dark she moved through her evenings with a tightening dread, checking locks repeatedly and keeping lights on longer than she needed, because the hours after sunset carried the sense that something terrible could happen again.

The event that had fractured this sense of safety dated back decades, when Trang was taken and held captive during a period of political violence in Southeast Asia before she came to the United States. She rarely described the full details in one sitting, but the fragments she gave were vivid enough: being ordered into a confined space, not knowing whether she would be released, the humiliation of having no control over her own body or movements, and the slow, corrosive certainty that the people in authority would not protect her. What remained with her most sharply was not only the fear of the captivity itself, but the feeling that those who should have safeguarded her had failed her completely. In the years that followed, she came to believe that she had been left alone to endure something no person should have had to survive, and that belief colored everything that came after.

That conviction fed directly into the way Trang experienced herself now. She spoke with bitterness and shame about how the event had changed her, saying that she felt dirty, contaminated, as if what had happened had left a stain that ordinary washing could not remove. She was equally harsh toward her own capacity to manage ordinary stress, insisting that she could not deal with even the slightest upset. A minor disagreement at work, a late bill, or a change in her schedule could leave her rattled for hours. Those appraisals made the world feel even more dangerous to her; if she had been abandoned once and had survived by sheer luck, then she felt she could be overwhelmed again by anything that disrupted her fragile order. The more she saw herself as damaged and easily undone, the more every unfamiliar place, every unexpected sound, and every darkened street seemed to confirm that the threat was still present.

In response to that sense of danger, Trang tried hard not to think about the captivity at all. She pushed the memories away whenever they began to surface, filling silence with work tasks, television, or practical errands. At night she delayed sleep until very late, telling herself she was catching up on emails or balancing accounts, though in truth she was avoiding the moment when the apartment would grow quiet and the old fear would swell. She also found herself caught in counterfactual thinking, replaying the past with painful precision and wondering how life would have been different if the event had never occurred. She imagined a version of herself who slept normally, trusted people more easily, and did not live with the constant edge of dread. Yet these efforts to keep the memories and feelings at bay never settled her for long; the more she fought them, the more strongly the fear returned, and the more certain she became that she had been permanently altered by what had happened.

Trang's daytime life at the financial firm became increasingly shaped by this cycle. She was known as meticulous and dependable, but she began avoiding after-hours meetings and any assignment that would keep her downtown after dark. If she had to stay late, she moved with palpable tension, watching the parking lot and the lobby for signs of threat. She had once enjoyed a sense of competence in her work, but now every small disruption felt like proof of her fragility, and that belief deepened her conviction that she could not cope. Her attempts to suppress the memories, keep busy, and stay up late provided only brief relief; afterward, she felt more on edge, more physically alert, and more certain that the world was unsafe. The fear sharpened her wish to avoid thinking about the trauma, and the avoidance in turn made the threat feel ever closer, as if the danger were lying in wait just beyond the edge of her attention.

By the time she sought help, Trang was exhausted by this narrowing existence. She said she was frightened most by the thought that the nights would continue to belong to the trauma, that her life would keep shrinking around safe rooms and locked doors, and that she would never again feel clean, settled, or capable of facing even small disruptions without falling apart. What brought her in was not a single crisis but the realization that, despite years of managing on her own, she was living as though captivity were still governing her days.
